The composer Clara Schumann is often remembered as the wife of Robert Schumann and the performer who championed his music. Musicologist Ingrid Bauer argues that this framing understates Clara Schumann’s own role as a composer. Her piano concerto, written when she was fourteen, was praised by contemporaries for its original orchestration, and her later songs were admired for their harmonic daring. Bauer does not deny that Clara Schumann promoted her husband’s work; she contends that remembering her only as a promoter erases a composing career that was recognized in its own time.

Which choice best states Bauer’s argument?
options: Contemporaries ignored Clara Schumann’s compositions entirely and never praised her piano concerto or songs at all in her lifetime.
Robert Schumann’s music was less original than his wife’s early concerto and later songs combined in every way.
Clara Schumann wrote her piano concerto only after her husband’s death, when she was already an established performer.
Clara Schumann should be remembered as a composer in her own right, not only as her husband’s promoter and performer.
explanation:
Step 1: Bauer concedes Clara promoted Robert’s work but argues the “wife and promoter” framing understates her composing: a concerto at fourteen praised for original orchestration, later songs admired for harmonic daring.

Step 2: Her claim is that remembering her only as promoter erases a recognized composing career — Choice D.

Choice C is unsupported: the concerto was written at fourteen, with no death timeline given. Choice A contradicts the passage: contemporaries praised her work. Choice B is a comparison Bauer never makes.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Psychologists have long debated whether people make better decisions alone or in groups. A series of experiments found a subtle pattern: groups outperformed individuals on problems with a demonstrably correct answer, such as logic puzzles, because one member who found the solution could show the others why it was right. On problems with no single correct answer, such as estimating the value of a painting, groups did no better than individuals and sometimes did worse, because confident but mistaken members could sway the group. The advantage of groups, then, depends on whether correctness can be demonstrated.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Groups always make better decisions than individuals on every kind of problem, whether or not answers can be demonstrated.
Individuals always outperform groups on logic puzzles, even when one member finds the correct solution quickly.
Confident group members are always correct about the value of paintings, even when they have no evidence.
Groups outperform individuals only when a correct answer can be demonstrated to the group; otherwise they offer no advantage.
explanation:
Step 1: The pattern has two branches: demonstrably correct problems (logic puzzles) → groups win, because a solver can demonstrate the answer; no single correct answer (painting value) → groups do no better and sometimes worse, because confident mistaken members sway others.

Step 2: Choice D states that conditional advantage exactly.

Choice A ignores the second branch. Choice B reverses the logic-puzzle finding. Choice C contradicts the passage: confident members could be mistaken and sway the group.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Archaeologists excavating a coastal settlement found two layers of debris. The lower layer contained fish bones, shells, and simple stone tools, suggesting a community that lived mainly from the sea. The upper layer contained wheat grains, pottery shards, and loom weights, suggesting farming and weaving. Some scholars concluded that a new farming people replaced the fishing community. Others argued that the same community gradually adopted farming while continuing to fish, pointing out that fish bones still appear, though in smaller numbers, in the upper layer. The continuing presence of fish bones weakens the replacement theory.

Which choice is best supported by the evidence described in the text?
options: Stone tools prove that the settlement never practiced farming and relied only on fishing throughout its entire history.
The settlement’s people stopped eating fish as soon as they began farming and never fished again after that.
The same community may have gradually adopted farming, since fish bones still appear in the upper layer alongside farming evidence.
The upper layer proves that the fishing community was completely replaced by farmers who brought wheat and pottery.
explanation:
Step 1: Map the layers: lower = fish, shells, stone tools (sea life); upper = wheat, pottery, loom weights (farming/weaving) plus fish bones in smaller numbers.

Step 2: Continued fish bones in the upper layer are evidence of continuity, weakening complete replacement — Choice C.

Choice D ignores the continuing fish bones. Choice B contradicts them: fish were still eaten, though less. Choice A is false: the upper layer’s wheat and loom weights show farming alongside the older stone-tool tradition.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
When a pharmaceutical company tested a new pain reliever, patients who received the drug reported an average pain reduction of 3 points on a 10-point scale, while patients who received a placebo reported an average reduction of 2 points. The difference was statistically significant, meaning it was unlikely to be due to chance. Yet the company’s own researchers noted that a 1-point difference is small in clinical terms: most patients would barely notice it. The trial thus shows a real but modest effect — a distinction between statistical significance and practical importance.

Which choice best captures the main point of the text?
options: The drug had no effect at all compared with the placebo, and patients in both groups reported identical pain reductions.
A 1-point difference on a 10-point scale is always a large clinical improvement that most patients would notice immediately.
The drug’s benefit over placebo was statistically significant but clinically small, so significance alone does not show a large practical effect.
The placebo was more effective than the drug at reducing pain, despite the drug’s statistically significant trial results.
explanation:
Step 1: The numbers: drug 3 points versus placebo 2 points — a 1-point gap that is statistically significant (unlikely due to chance).

Step 2: The researchers’ own judgment is that 1 point is small clinically and most patients would barely notice it — Choice C distinguishes statistical from practical significance.

Choice A contradicts the significant 1-point difference. Choice D reverses the numbers: the drug reduced pain more than placebo. Choice B contradicts the researchers’ judgment that the difference is small.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
In the early twentieth century, many American cities built grand public parks in the belief that green space would improve public health and morals. Historian Eleanor Vance notes a complication: the parks were often built in wealthy neighborhoods or on land that required expensive travel to reach, so the working-class residents they were meant to help used them least. Vance does not argue that parks failed as places of beauty; she argues that their benefits depended on who could actually reach them, and that access, not intention, determined their social effect.

Which choice best states Vance’s argument?
options: Public parks were ugly and unhealthy places that harmed everyone who visited them daily, regardless of their neighborhood or background.
Working-class residents used the parks more than any other group, despite the long and expensive travel they required each week.
The social benefit of public parks depended on who could reach them, and working-class residents often could not, despite good intentions.
Wealthy neighborhoods opposed the construction of public parks in their areas and tried to stop them being built there altogether.
explanation:
Step 1: Vance’s complication: parks were often in wealthy neighborhoods or hard to reach, so intended working-class users used them least.

Step 2: Her claim is that access, not intention, determined social effect — Choice C.

Choice A contradicts the passage: Vance does not deny parks’ beauty. Choice D is unsupported — no opposition from wealthy neighborhoods is mentioned. Choice B reverses the evidence: working-class residents used the parks least.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Two economists studied the same tax change and reached different conclusions about its effect on employment. The first compared employment in the year before the change with employment in the year after, and found a sharp increase. The second compared the state that changed its tax with a neighboring state that did not, over the same years, and found almost no difference between them. The second economist argued that the first study mistook a general economic recovery — which raised employment in both states — for an effect of the tax change. The disagreement turns on whether a comparison over time or a comparison between states is the better control.

Which choice best explains the disagreement?
options: The two economists studied different tax changes in different years, so their conclusions about employment cannot be compared directly at all by anyone.
The first study compared one state over time and mistook a general recovery for the tax effect; the second used a neighboring state as control.
Employment fell sharply in both states after the tax change, contradicting the findings of both economists’ studies on employment and their conclusions about jobs.
The neighboring state also changed its tax in the same year, so it could not serve as a valid control for comparing employment changes.
explanation:
Step 1: Identify the methods: study one is before-versus-after in one state (sharp increase); study two is changed-state versus unchanged neighboring state over the same years (almost no difference).

Step 2: The second economist’s critique is that a general recovery raised employment in both states, so the time comparison confounds recovery with tax effect — Choice B.

Choice A contradicts the text: both studied the same tax change over the same years. Choice D contradicts the premise that the neighbor did not change its tax. Choice C contradicts both findings: employment rose, and the second study found almost no difference.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
The writer Zora Neale Hurston once observed that research is “formalized curiosity.” In her anthropological fieldwork in the American South, she collected folktales not by interrogating strangers but by joining in conversations, telling stories of her own, and earning trust over weeks. Scholars who later read her field notes have noted that this method produced richer material than a questionnaire would have, but also that it blurred the line between observer and participant: the stories people told Hurston were shaped by the relationship she had built with them. Her work thus raises a question that still divides anthropologists — whether closeness to a community deepens understanding or distorts it.

Which choice best states the central idea of the text?
options: Hurston’s fieldwork produced rich material but blurred the observer-participant line, raising the question of whether closeness deepens or distorts understanding.
Hurston’s fieldwork was less effective than questionnaires at collecting folktales from southern communities she studied over many weeks.
Anthropologists agree that closeness to a community always distorts research and completely prevents any reliable understanding by outsiders.
Hurston never earned the trust of the communities she studied, despite spending weeks joining their conversations and stories.
explanation:
Step 1: Hurston’s method: joining conversations, telling her own stories, earning trust over weeks — producing richer material than a questionnaire.

Step 2: The trade-off noted by scholars is that the relationship shaped the stories, blurring observer and participant, leaving open whether closeness deepens or distorts understanding — Choice A.

Choice B reverses the scholars’ judgment that her method produced richer material. Choice D contradicts the passage: she earned trust over weeks. Choice C contradicts the text: the question still divides anthropologists, so there is no agreement.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Mara watches the geese return to the lake every autumn.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The flock of geese migrates across the lake each autumn.
The flock of geese migrate across the lake each autumn.
The flock of geese migrating across the lake each autumn.
The flock of geese migrates across the lake each autumn, the birds fly in a V shape.
explanation: The subject is the singular collective noun 'flock,' so it takes the singular verb 'migrates,' not the plural 'migrate.' A participle phrase such as 'migrating across the lake' has no finite main verb, so that version is a fragment. Joining two independent clauses ('The flock ... migrates ...' and 'the birds fly ...') with only a comma is a comma splice.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
The playground was empty until the clouds finally broke.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: After the rain stopped the children ran outside to play.
After the rain stopped, the children ran outside to play.
After the rain stopped, the children running outside to play.
After the rain stopped, the children ran outside to played.
explanation: An introductory clause ('After the rain stopped') must be followed by a comma before the main clause, so the version with no comma is wrong. The main clause also needs a finite verb: 'running' is a participle, so that version is a fragment. And the infinitive after 'to' takes the base form 'play,' not the past-tense form 'played.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
The museum added weekend programs to welcome more visitors.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: The museum extended it's hours on weekends to welcome more visitors.
The museum extended their hours on weekends to welcome more visitors.
The museum extended its hours on weekends to welcome more visitors.
The museum extended its hours on weekends to welcomed more visitors.
explanation: The possessive form is 'its' (no apostrophe); 'it's' is the contraction of 'it is,' which makes no sense here. The museum is a singular noun, so the plural pronoun 'their' does not agree with it. Finally, the infinitive marker 'to' must be followed by the base verb 'welcome,' not the past form 'welcomed.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A food critic is reviewing a small restaurant in the neighborhood.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The chefs new menu features dishes from her grandmother's kitchen.
The chef's new menu features dishes from her grandmothers kitchen.
The chefs' new menu features dishes from her grandmother's kitchen.
The chef's new menu features dishes from her grandmother's kitchen.
explanation: One chef owns the menu, so the singular possessive 'chef's' is required; 'chefs' with no apostrophe shows no possession at all, and 'chefs'' is the possessive of more than one chef, which contradicts the singular 'her.' Likewise, the kitchen belongs to one grandmother, so it needs the singular possessive 'grandmother's.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Lena had a busy afternoon after school.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Yesterday, Lena finished her homework and walks the dog.
Yesterday, Lena finished her homework and walked the dog.
Yesterday, Lena finishes her homework and walked the dog.
Yesterday, Lena finished her homework and walking the dog.
explanation: The time marker 'Yesterday' puts the whole sentence in the past, so both verbs must be past tense: 'finished' and 'walked.' Switching either verb to the present ('walks' or 'finishes') breaks tense consistency, and 'walking' is a participle, not a finite past-tense verb parallel to 'finished.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A hardware store sells a beginner's tool set.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: The kit contains a hammer, a screwdriver, and a wrench.
The kit contains a hammer a screwdriver and a wrench.
The kit contains a hammer, a screwdriver and, a wrench.
The kit contains a hammer, a screwdriver, and a wrenches.
explanation: Items in a list must be separated by commas, with a comma before 'and' in the final item, so the version with no commas at all is wrong. The comma in the second wrong choice is misplaced after 'and' instead of before it. And the article 'a' requires the singular noun 'wrench,' not the plural 'wrenches.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
The librarian is shelving books that were returned this morning.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The books on the shelf belongs to the library.
The books on the shelf belonging to the library.
The books on the shelf belong to the library.
The books on the shelf belong to the library, they are due back Friday.
explanation: The subject is the plural noun 'books,' so the verb must be the plural 'belong'; the singular 'belongs' wrongly agrees with 'shelf,' which is only the object of the preposition 'on.' The participle 'belonging' gives the sentence no finite main verb, making it a fragment. And joining two independent clauses with only a comma is a comma splice.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A cooking class is preparing a simple dessert.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: The recipe needs three ingredients, flour, sugar, and butter.
The recipe needs three ingredients; flour, sugar, and butter.
The recipe needs three ingredients flour, sugar, and butter.
The recipe needs three ingredients: flour, sugar, and butter.
explanation: A colon correctly introduces a list after a complete independent clause. A comma cannot introduce a list, a semicolon cannot introduce a list (it joins independent clauses or separates complex list items), and with no punctuation at all the list runs into the sentence ungrammatically.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A hiking club is planning a trip into the mountains.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The forecast predicted sunshine, however, the hikers packed rain jackets just in case.
The forecast predicted sunshine; however, the hikers packed rain jackets just in case.
The forecast predicted sunshine; however the hikers packed rain jackets just in case.
The forecast predicted sunshine however, the hikers packed rain jackets just in case.
explanation: Two independent clauses joined by the conjunctive adverb 'however' need a semicolon before 'however' and a comma after it. A comma before 'however' creates a comma splice, a semicolon without the comma after 'however' omits required punctuation, and no punctuation before 'however' leaves a run-on sentence.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A science magazine is profiling a researcher who studies coral reefs.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: Dr. Alvarez, a marine biologist, studies coral reefs off the coast of Belize.
Dr. Alvarez, a marine biologist studies coral reefs off the coast of Belize.
Dr. Alvarez a marine biologist, studies coral reefs off the coast of Belize.
Dr. Alvarez, a marine biologist, study coral reefs off the coast of Belize.
explanation: The appositive 'a marine biologist' is nonessential information, so it must be set off by a pair of commas, one before and one after; either comma alone leaves the phrase half-enclosed. The singular subject 'Dr. Alvarez' also requires the singular verb 'studies,' not the plural 'study.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Priya plans her weekends around outdoor activities.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: On weekends, Priya enjoys hiking, swimming, and to cycle.
On weekends, Priya enjoys hiking, swimming, and cycled.
On weekends, Priya enjoys hiking, swimming, and cycling.
On weekends, Priya enjoys hiking, swimming, and cycle.
explanation: Items in a series must be parallel in form: here all three activities are gerunds ('hiking,' 'swimming,' 'cycling'). An infinitive ('to cycle'), a past-tense verb ('cycled'), and a base-form verb ('cycle') each break that parallel structure.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Maya overslept on the morning of her exam.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: Running late for the bus, her backpack was grabbed by Maya and she sprinted out the door.
Running late for the bus Maya grabbed her backpack and sprinted out the door.
Running late for the bus, Maya grabbed her backpack, and sprinted out the door.
Running late for the bus, Maya grabbed her backpack and sprinted out the door.
explanation: The participial phrase 'Running late for the bus' must modify the subject that follows it, and Maya is the one running late, so the version that makes 'her backpack' the subject is a dangling modifier. An introductory participial phrase must also be followed by a comma. Finally, no comma belongs before 'and' in a compound predicate ('grabbed ... and sprinted ...') with a single subject.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Elena and Rosa met at the train station, where one of them had a book to deliver.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: When Elena met Rosa at the station, she handed her a copy of the novel.
When Elena met Rosa at the station, Elena handed Rosa a copy of the novel.
When Elena met Rosa at the station, she handed Rosa a copy of the novel.
When Elena met Rosa at the station, Rosa handed her a copy of the novel.
explanation: With two women in the sentence, the pronouns 'she' and 'her' have no clear antecedent, so each pronoun version is ambiguous about who gave the book and who received it. Repeating the names 'Elena' and 'Rosa' is the only version that makes the actor and the recipient unmistakable.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Aunt Mei sent a present for the holidays.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: The box of chocolates on the counter was a gift from Aunt Mei.
The box of chocolates on the counter were a gift from Aunt Mei.
The box of chocolates on the counter being a gift from Aunt Mei.
The box of chocolates on the counter was a gift from Aunt Mei, she thanked her.
explanation: The subject is the singular noun 'box,' so the verb must be the singular 'was'; the plural 'were' wrongly agrees with 'chocolates,' which is only the object of the preposition 'of.' The participle 'being' leaves the sentence without a finite main verb, making it a fragment, and joining two independent clauses with only a comma is a comma splice.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
The orchestra was ready long before the curtain rose.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: By the time the concert began, the audience has already taken their seats.
By the time the concert began, the audience already took their seats.
By the time the concert began, the audience had already taken their seats.
By the time the concert began, the audience had already took their seats.
explanation: The seating happened before the past-tense event 'the concert began,' so it requires the past perfect 'had taken.' The present perfect 'has taken' clashes with the past time frame, the simple past 'took' does not mark the action as completed before the concert began, and 'took' is the wrong past participle after 'had' (the correct form is 'taken').
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
An astronomy club is describing its observatory on a hilltop.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: The observatory has one major limitation, its dome cannot open during high winds.
The observatory has one major limitation its dome cannot open during high winds.
The observatory has one major limitation: its dome cannot opened during high winds.
The observatory has one major limitation: its dome cannot open during high winds.
explanation: A colon correctly follows a complete independent clause to introduce an explanation of that clause. A comma joining two independent clauses is a comma splice, no punctuation at all leaves a run-on, and after the modal 'cannot' the verb must be the base form 'open,' not the past form 'opened.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A sailor keeps an old lighthouse in working order.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The old lighthouse — built in 1890 still guides ships safely into the harbor.
The old lighthouse — built in 1890 — still guides ships safely into the harbor.
The old lighthouse built in 1890 — still guides ships safely into the harbor.
The old lighthouse — built in 1890 — still guide ships safely into the harbor.
explanation: A parenthetical phrase set off with dashes needs a matching pair, one dash before and one after it; either dash alone leaves the interruption unclosed. The singular subject 'lighthouse' also requires the singular verb 'guides,' not the plural 'guide.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A novelist is scheduled to visit the town library tonight.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: The author whose novel won the prize will speak at the library tonight.
The author who's novel won the prize will speak at the library tonight.
The author whose novel won the prize will spoke at the library tonight.
The author whose novel won the prize will speaks at the library tonight.
explanation: The possessive relative pronoun is 'whose'; 'who's' is the contraction of 'who is,' which makes no sense before 'novel.' After the modal 'will,' the verb must be the base form 'speak,' not the past form 'spoke' or the third-person singular 'speaks.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
The town council has just opened a new building for residents.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The new community center is not only a library but also meeting local clubs.
The new community center is not only a library but also meets local clubs.
The new community center is not only a library but also a meeting place for local clubs.
The new community center is not only a library but also a meeting places for local clubs.
explanation: The correlative pair 'not only ... but also' must join parallel elements: here both are noun phrases ('a library' and 'a meeting place for local clubs'). A gerund phrase ('meeting local clubs') and a verb phrase ('meets local clubs') break that parallelism, and the article 'a' requires the singular noun 'place,' not the plural 'places.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
The crew waited for the weather to change before setting sail.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: The wind died down and the sailors raised the sails.
The wind died down, the sailors raised the sails.
The wind died down; and the sailors raised the sails.
The wind died down, and the sailors raised the sails.
explanation: Two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction 'and' need a comma before 'and.' With no comma, the join is missing required punctuation; with only a comma and no conjunction, it is a comma splice; and a semicolon must never be followed by a coordinating conjunction such as 'and.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
At the annual school fair, dozens of children showed their work to visitors.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The student's science projects were displayed in the main hall.
The students' science projects were displayed in the main hall.
The students science projects were displayed in the main hall.
The students' science projects was displayed in the main hall.
explanation: Many students own the projects, so the plural possessive 'students'' is required; the singular possessive 'student's' refers to only one student, and 'students' with no apostrophe shows no possession at all. The plural subject 'projects' also requires the plural verb 'were,' not the singular 'was.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A shop owner is writing the closing duties on a notice board.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: Either the manager or the assistants are responsible for closing the shop.
Either the manager or the assistants is responsible for closing the shop.
Either the manager or the assistants are responsible for close the shop.
Either the manager or the assistants being responsible for closing the shop.
explanation: In an 'either ... or' construction, the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it, which is the plural 'assistants,' so the plural 'are' is required, not the singular 'is.' After the preposition 'for,' the verb must take the gerund form 'closing,' not the base form 'close,' and the participle 'being' leaves the sentence without a finite main verb, making it a fragment.
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A harbor guide is describing the oldest building on the point.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Built in 1890 the lighthouse still guides ships into the harbor.
Built in 1890, the ships are still guided by the lighthouse into the harbor.
Built in 1890, the lighthouse still guides ships into the harbor.
Built in 1890, the lighthouse still guide ships into the harbor.
explanation: An introductory participial phrase must be followed by a comma, so the version with no comma is wrong. The phrase 'Built in 1890' must modify the lighthouse, not the ships, so making 'the ships' the subject is a dangling modifier. And the singular subject 'lighthouse' requires the singular verb 'guides,' not the plural 'guide.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
The team lost the championship game by a single point.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Neither the coach nor the players was surprised by the final score.
Neither the coach nor the players were surprised by the final score, they had practiced all season.
Neither the coach nor the players were surprising by the final score.
Neither the coach nor the players were surprised by the final score.
explanation: In a 'neither ... nor' construction, the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it, which is the plural 'players,' so the plural 'were' is required, not the singular 'was.' Joining two independent clauses with only a comma is a comma splice, and the passive construction requires the past participle 'surprised,' not the present participle 'surprising.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
The museum board is debating whether to fund a new education wing.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: If the committee was to approve the plan, the museum would expand its education wing.
If the committee were to approve the plan, the museum would expand its education wing.
If the committee were to approve the plan, the museum will expand its education wing.
If the committee were to approve the plan, the museum would expanded its education wing.
explanation: A hypothetical 'if' clause requires the subjunctive 'were,' not the indicative 'was.' The result clause must stay in the conditional mood with 'would,' so 'will' breaks the conditional sequence, and after the modal 'would' the verb must be the base form 'expand,' not the past form 'expanded.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A company is reviewing a plan to cut operating expenses.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: The proposal aims to reduce costs, to improve safety, and to increase efficiency.
The proposal aims to reduce costs, improving safety, and to increase efficiency.
The proposal aims to reduce costs, to improve safety, and increasing efficiency.
The proposal aims to reduce costs, to improve safety, and to increased efficiency.
explanation: All three items in the series must be parallel infinitives: 'to reduce,' 'to improve,' and 'to increase.' A gerund ('improving' or 'increasing') breaks that parallelism, and after 'to' the verb must be the base form 'increase,' not the past form 'increased.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A hiring manager is comparing two candidates for an internship.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: The new intern is as qualified as her is, and her references confirm it.
The new intern is as qualified as her, and her references confirm it.
The new intern is as qualified as she is, and her references confirm it.
The new intern is as qualified as she is, and their references confirm it.
explanation: In the elliptical comparison 'as she is,' the pronoun is the subject of the understood clause, so it must be the subject form 'she,' not the object form 'her,' whether the verb 'is' is stated or omitted. The intern is also singular, so the singular possessive 'her' is required, not the plural 'their.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Mara trained all spring for a long-distance race.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: Mara had one goal for the summer; to finish the marathon before sunset.
Mara had one goal for the summer to finish the marathon before sunset.
Mara had one goal for the summer: to finished the marathon before sunset.
Mara had one goal for the summer: to finish the marathon before sunset.
explanation: A colon correctly follows a complete independent clause to introduce an appositive infinitive phrase that names the goal. A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, not a phrase, so it cannot be used here; no punctuation at all leaves a run-on; and after 'to' the verb must be the base form 'finish,' not the past form 'finished.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
A librarian has finally finished sorting a collection found in an old house.

Which choice is grammatically correct?
options: Covered in dust, the old manuscripts, which had been stored in the attic, was finally catalogued.
Covered in dust, the old manuscripts, which had been stored in the attic, were finally catalogued.
Covered in dust, the old manuscripts which had been stored in the attic were finally catalogued.
Covered in dust, the old manuscripts, which had been stored in the attic, were finally cataloguing.
explanation: The subject is the plural noun 'manuscripts,' so the verb must be the plural 'were,' not the singular 'was.' The relative clause 'which had been stored in the attic' is nonessential, so it must be enclosed by a pair of commas; with no commas it wrongly reads as essential. And the passive construction requires the past participle 'catalogued,' not the present participle 'cataloguing.'
subject: Reading & Writing

text:
Scientists have been tracking a glacier in the far north for decades.

Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?
options: When the researchers published their findings, they noted that the glacier had retreated more than 10 miles since 1980.
When the researchers published their findings, they noted that the glacier has retreated more than 10 miles since 1980.
When the researchers published their findings, they noted that the glacier had retreat more than 10 miles since 1980.
When the researchers published their findings, they noted that the glacier retreated more than 10 miles since 1980.
explanation: The retreat began before the past-tense reporting ('published' and 'noted') and continued up to that point, so it requires the past perfect 'had retreated.' The present perfect 'has retreated' clashes with the past-tense frame, 'retreat' is the wrong participle after 'had' (the correct form is 'retreated'), and the simple past 'retreated' cannot combine with 'since 1980,' which requires a perfect tense.
subject: Reading & Writing
